title: Two thousand NetworkPolicies and a network that gave up
role: You are an SRE for a large wiki platform. Its application servers run on Kubernetes with Calico, and engineers have just started running maintenance scripts as Kubernetes jobs through a new self-service tool.
brief: 05:01 UTC. Logged-in users, edits and API calls are slow or failing in the primary datacenter, while cached page views look fine. GatewayBackendErrorsHigh fires, then KubernetesCalicoDown on 16 instances.

steps.situation: The cluster network itself is failing.
steps.evidence:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep -E 'calico-kube|typha' | head -2
calico-kube-controllers-5c7d9-xk2  0/1  CrashLoopBackOff  12
calico-typha-7f8c4-q9w             1/1  Running           3
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=calico-node | grep -c ' 0/1 '
61

choices.text: Find what changed: count NetworkPolicies and jobs per namespace
choices.why: Calico's work grows with the number of policies and endpoints it must program. A sudden jump in objects is a prime suspect.

choices.text: Restart every calico-node pod at once
choices.why: Every node loses its network programming at the same moment, and the pods come back to the same load.
Their pods move onto nodes whose Calico is just as overloaded.

steps.evidence:
$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A --no-headers | wc -l
1968
$ kubectl -n mw-script get jobs --no-headers | wc -l
1791
$ helm -n mw-script list --short | wc -l
1790

choices.text: Ask the operator to pause new script runs, and raise Calico's limits through the normal helmfile deploy
choices.why: Each run of the tool deploys a whole Helm release with its own policies. Stopping new runs stops the growth; more resources let Calico catch up.

choices.text: Only raise Calico's limits through helmfile
choices.why: That's what responders did, and Calico recovered. But the source keeps growing while you wait.
You remove the jobs' network protection, fight Helm, which owns those objects, and leave the scripts half done.

steps.situation: 06:05. Someone proposes moving traffic to the secondary datacenter. Calico pods are coming back, and it's unclear whether a switchover is safe for the databases.

choices.text: Prepare the read-only services to move, ask the database team, and keep watching recovery
choices.why: You keep the option ready without taking a risk you can't size. By 06:07, 212 calico-node pods were ready.
A big move with open questions about replication, just as the primary recovers.
Users and other teams need to know what's happening and what you're weighing.

steps.situation: The post-incident review: what should change?

choices.text: One shared NetworkPolicy for script jobs, concurrency limits in the tool, and alerts on object counts
choices.why: Self-service needs guardrails: the tool shouldn't be able to create thousands of objects, and you want to see the growth hours before Calico falls over.

choices.text: Keep the higher Calico limits and move on
choices.why: It raises the ceiling. The next bigger batch hits it again.

choices.text: Take the tool away from the operator who ran it
choices.why: They used a supported tool as designed. The design is what failed.

debrief.what_happened: On 9 October 2024, from about 05:01 to 06:10 UTC, uncached traffic in Wikimedia's primary datacenter (codfw) saw high latency and errors. An operator was running a transcode maintenance script in batches through the new mwscript-k8s tool, and every invocation deployed a Helm release with its own jobs and NetworkPolicies. Nearly 2,000 Calico NetworkPolicies piled up, the namespace held 1,791 jobs by about 06:30, and etcd ConfigMaps roughly doubled, from about 6k to 12k. Calico controllers, Typha and calico-node hit their resource limits, were throttled and failed, taking nodes out of rotation. GatewayBackendErrorsHigh and KubernetesCalicoDown alerted the on-call. Around 06:00 a responder deployed higher Calico limits through helmfile, and by 06:07 212 calico-node pods were ready; the report says it's unclear whether the limits or the redeploy fixed it. Moving traffic to the other datacenter was discussed, but whether that was safe was unclear. Follow-up T376795 covers mwscript-k8s creating too many resources, with ideas such as one shared NetworkPolicy for scripts and concurrency limits.
lessons: Count objects: the control plane and CNI scale with them, not just with traffic.
Stop the source of growth as well as adding capacity.
Self-service tools need quotas and shared resources by design.
Failover is an option to prepare, not a reflex.
